schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the title 'words of Nehemiah' as deeds and history (as with David, Solomon, Jeroboam); Ellicott fixes the calendar and identifies Shushan as Susa, the winter residence of the Persian kings.

Clarke, following Prideaux, dates the mission to the twentieth year of Artaxerxes Longimanus (~445 BC) and the cupbearer's place at court; Wesley glosses 'words' as acts and Shushan as the royal city.
Gill takes 'dibre' of deeds as well as words, leaves Hachaliah's line unknown, and judges Nehemiah of the tribe of Judah, later the king's cupbearer.
Henry marks Nehemiah's modesty about his office and God's remnant in every place (Obadiah in Ahab's house, saints in Caesar's household), courts made sanctuaries to the church.

themes: the words and deeds of Nehemiah

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott identify Hanani as Nehemiah's own brother (Neh. 7:2), come from the province of Judah, and read 'the escaped' as the returned remnant set against those still in heathen lands.

Henry reads the enquiry as compassion undimmed by dignity or difference of practice; like Moses (Acts 7:23) Nehemiah in spirit visited his brethren, inquiring after the church's state to guide his prayers (not the Athenians of Acts 17:21).
Clarke supplies Josephus's scene: Nehemiah near Susa overhears strangers speaking Hebrew and asks the men from Jerusalem how their brethren fare.
Gill allows Hanani a brother or fellow-Jew, citing Jarchi's reading of him as a companion or acquaintance.

Ellicott hears the pathos of 'the escaped' and 'the remnant that are left' and reads the wall as still prostrate since Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:10); Keil reports the divided opinion but notes Rambach's reply that no rebuilding by Zerubbabel or Ezra is recorded.

Henry (with Hanani who feared God, Neh. 7:2) reads the twofold report — the holy seed trampled and the holy city exposed — and the one good work still undone, every Jerusalem below the heavenly one having some defect.

Clarke argues the broken wall must be a later demolition, the Babylonian ruin being no news to Nehemiah; Wesley reads it plainly as still lying as Nebuchadnezzar left it, the Jews unable and uncommissioned to rebuild.
Gill fixes 'the province' as Judea, now reduced to a province of the Persian empire.

debates.question: Does the broken-down wall Hanani reports date from Nebuchadnezzar's original overthrow, or from a later demolition?

sides.position: The ancient Babylonian ruin, never rebuilt — the walls still lie as Nebuchadnezzar left them
A later demolition of walls rebuilt after the return, since the old ruin was no news to Nehemiah

themes: the remnant in affliction and reproach
the broken wall and burned gates

schools.summary: Henry reads a grief that continued days and turned Godward: fasting and praying before the God who sees in secret, consecrating his sorrows and taking God along in the first conception of every good design.

Clarke measures the mourning from Chisleu to Nisan (Neh. 2:1), some four months of supplication and waiting on providence, warning that good works are ruined by haste; Wesley marks the God of heaven who sees in secret.
Gill notes simply the sad and melancholy account that moved him.

themes: fasting before the God of heaven
no good work undertaken in haste

schools.summary: Henry finds in the address (much like Daniel 9:4) a pattern of drawing near — holy awe of the great and terrible God, whose very terrors comfort those who trust him, joined to holy confidence in a God who keeps covenant beyond his promise.

Keil and Delitzsch root each epithet in the law — 'great and terrible' (Deut. 7:21), 'keepest covenant and mercy' (Deut. 7:9; Exod. 20:6) — and gather the prayer as the sum of Nehemiah's day-and-night supplications.
Clarke reads the pre-exilic 'Jehovah, God of hosts' confessed afresh: great to do mighty things, terrible to inflict the heaviest judgments.
Gill notes Nehemiah prayed not to the host of heaven or the sun the Persians adored, but to the God of heaven, humbly.

themes: the God of heaven, not the host of heaven
great and terrible, yet keeping covenant

schools.summary: Henry distinguishes saying a prayer from praying it, appeals to the God who formed the eye and planted the ear, and reads 'I and my father's house have sinned' as a penitent's willingness to name himself first among the offenders.

Keil and Delitzsch match 'let thine ear be attentive, thine eyes open' to Solomon's temple prayer (2 Chron. 6:40; 7:15), render the term 'now' rather than 'this day,' and mark the move from communal to personal confession.
Gill takes the opening as a plain cry that God's ear be attentive to the prayer now made.

themes: I and my father's house have sinned

schools.summary: Henry names the double malignity of sin — a corruption of ourselves and an affront to God — and reads the honest 'we have not kept' as itself laying the ground of a plea to the God who gave both command and promise through Moses.
Keil and Delitzsch weigh the intensive infinitive and gloss 'dealt corruptly' as precisely the failure to keep the commandments, statutes, and judgments.
Clarke sorts the three terms — commandments the moral precepts, statutes the rites and ceremonies, judgments the precepts of justice between men — a breach running through the whole law.
Gill reads the corrupt dealing as a corrupting of God's covenant, laws, and precepts, contrary to his nature, mind, and will.
Keil and Delitzsch unfold the threat-and-promise structure — scatter for sin, gather on repentance to the chosen place — and mark the word as part of the covenant law commanded to Moses.

Henry shows the threat fulfilled in the dispersion become a plea, since the same word promised regathering (Deut. 30:1); the best pleas in prayer are drawn from God's promise, the word on which he causes us to hope (Ps. 119:49).
Clarke traces the citation to Lev. 26:33 and Deut. 4:27; 28:64, praising Nehemiah's accuracy though far from the ordinances of God.
Gill notes Nehemiah asks God to remember the word commanded Moses to publish to Israel.

themes: if ye transgress, I will scatter

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch carry the ingathering to the ends of heaven and the chosen place, and mark how the prayer widens to include all God's servants who delight to fear his name.
Henry weighs the condition and comfort: repentance begun in renounced idolatry, and the distance of Deut. 30:4 put in to magnify a mercy that no dispersion is too wide to reach.
Gill reads 'if ye return' as repentance proved by a yielding and continuing obedience.

themes: gathered from the ends of heaven

schools.summary: Henry builds a double argument — the covenant relation of sworn servants against sworn enemies (Isa. 63:19) and the ancient redemption by great power, still the same — as ground for present mercy.
Keil and Delitzsch set the words within the prayer's closing movement, laying hold of the people as God's own, redeemed by his great power and strong hand.
Gill identifies the servants and people as the remnant gathered from several countries and returned to Jerusalem and Judah.

Clarke reads a silent prayer offered as the cup passed to the king and expounds the cupbearer's trust and peril; Wesley marks 'this man' as but a man whose heart is at God's disposal, and the gracious acceptance of those who desire to fear God's name.

Henry insists the mercy sought is not the king's but God's in the approach to the king ('who art thou, that thou shouldest be afraid of a man?', Ps. 9:20), favour with men comfortable only when traced to the mercy of God.
Keil and Delitzsch note how the prayer widens to God's servants who delight to fear his name, then narrows to 'prosper thy servant this day.'
Gill takes the renewed cry as Nehemiah pressing home the petition he had been making all this while.

themes: mercy in the sight of this man
a king's heart at God's disposal
